heading_path: 1.5 Epidemiology of Tuberculosis > 1.5.1-1.5.2 Global Trends in TB Incidence and Mortality
text:
### Figures 1-2. Global TB incidence and mortality trends (WHO Global TB Report 2024): 10.8 million fell ill and 1.1 million died in 2023

Figure 1 (global TB incidence trends) and Figure 2 (global TB mortality trends) are line charts from the WHO Global TB Report 2024: (a) numbers in millions per year and (b) rates per 100,000 population, for all TB cases / notifications / TB in people with HIV, and total TB deaths / deaths in people with HIV / in HIV-negative people, 2010-2023, with End TB milestone lines.
Key figures stated in the text: in 2023 an estimated 10.8 million people fell ill with TB, including 1.3 million children; 6.8% were people living with HIV; TB caused about 1.1 million deaths; about 400,000 people fell ill with drug-resistant TB. About 25% of the world's population is infected with TB.

heading_path: 1.5 Epidemiology of Tuberculosis > TB in Eswatini
text:
### Figures 3-4. Drivers of TB in Eswatini (cases attributable to HIV, alcohol, smoking, undernutrition, diabetes) and estimated TB incidence and deaths 2010-2023

Figure 3 is a bar chart of the estimated number of TB cases in Eswatini attributable to five risk factors in 2023 (HIV, alcohol use disorders, smoking, undernutrition, diabetes), with uncertainty bounds; HIV is by far the largest. Figure 4 shows the estimated TB incidence rate and number of TB deaths in Eswatini, 2010-2023 (WHO Global TB Report 2024).
Key figures stated in the text: TB incidence fell from 1590/100,000 in 2010 to 335/100,000 in 2020; TB mortality in HIV-negative people fell from 56/100,000 (2010) to 24/100,000 (2020); progress was interrupted by COVID-19. In 2023 the incidence was 350/100,000, with an estimated 4300 people falling ill, 53.5% of them living with HIV. DR-TB incidence was 18/100,000 (230 people). HIV prevalence was 24.7% (SHIMS 3, 2021); 55% of notified cases were male in 2022.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Tuberculosis Case Finding > 3.7 TB Screening Algorithms with CXR and CAD/AI Use > Figure 11: PLHIV 15+ at Facilities with X-ray and CAD/AI
text:
### Figure 11. TB screening algorithm for PLHIV aged 15+ at facilities with X-ray and CAD/AI: symptom screen, CXR in past 12 months, CAD result, sputum Xpert + urine LF-LAM, TPT

Population: PLHIV adolescents >15 years and adults (old and new) attending health facilities.
1. Symptom screen (multi-entry): current cough OR fever OR weight loss OR night sweats.
   - Positive: collect two sputum samples and 1 urine sample**; perform microbiological assessment for active TB (Xpert and LF-LAM).
   - Negative: check if CXR screening was done in the past 12 months.
     - Yes: further clinical evaluation***; provide TPT if eligible.
     - No: X-ray screen with CAD → positive: collect sputum ×2 + urine for Xpert and LF-LAM; negative: further clinical evaluation***, TPT if eligible; non-TB abnormalities*: further clinical evaluation***, TPT if eligible.
2. Microbiological result: positive → initiate TB treatment; negative → further clinical evaluation***, provide TPT if eligible.
* Abnormalities e.g. cardiomegaly, possible cancer, silicosis. ** A urine sample is collected from every client with advanced HIV disease (AHD) for LF-LAM regardless of symptoms or CAD result. *** Further clinical evaluation includes clinical assessment of resolution of TB symptoms, re-reading of the CXR by a trained clinician, and further management/specialist referral as required; if on re-reading the CXR is suggestive of TB, evaluate for TB.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Tuberculosis Case Finding > 3.7 TB Screening Algorithms with CXR and CAD/AI Use > Figure 12: PLHIV 15+ at Facilities with X-ray, CAD/AI and CRP
text:
### Figure 12. TB screening algorithm for PLHIV aged 15+ at ART clinics with X-ray, CAD/AI and CRP: symptom screen, CRP for those not on ART, CXR with CAD for those on ART, Xpert, TB-LAM for AHD, TPT

Population: PLHIV (>15 years) attending ART clinics.
1. Symptom screen: current cough OR fever OR weight loss OR night sweats (WSS)*.
   - Yes: collect two sputum samples; perform Xpert for active TB diagnosis*.
   - No: is the individual on ART?
     - Not on ART: C-reactive protein screen → positive: collect two sputum samples for Xpert*; negative: evaluate for TPT eligibility and offer TPT if eligible.
     - On ART: was CXR screening done in the past 12 months? Yes: (no next step drawn). No: X-ray screen with CAD → positive**: (no next step drawn); non-TB abnormal#: further clinical evaluation, TPT if eligible; negative: further clinical evaluation, TPT if eligible.
2. Xpert result: positive → initiate TB treatment; negative → further clinical evaluation, TPT if eligible.
* Perform TB-LAM for all with AHD (CD4 <200, WHO stage 3 or 4 regardless of symptoms; seriously ill regardless of CD4; all presumptive TB regardless of CD4). ** If CAD reports silicosis, refer for assessment and treatment of silicosis and provide TPT if eligible. # Abnormal (not TB): e.g. cardiomegaly, possible cancer, silicosis (if smoking history and possible cancer on CXR, highly suspicious of cancer).

| 2 | Hold the air for 5 seconds |
| 3 | Breathe out slowly |
| 4 | Repeat steps 1-3 three times |
| 5 | Cough out hard from the chest |
| 6 | Spit sputum into plastic bottle |

heading_path: Chapter 4: TB and Drug-Resistant TB Diagnosis > 4.3 Microbiological diagnosis of TB and DR-TB
text:
### 4.3 Microbiological diagnosis of TB and DR-TB (MTB was Detected and Rifampicin resistance not detected)

Upon receiving the Xpert results, treatment decisions should be made as follows:

| MTB was Detected and Rifampicin resistance not detected |
| --- |
| (All patients whose diagnosis of TB has been confirmed by Xpert® MTB/RIF Ultra but without evidence of Rifampicin resistance) |
| Should be registered as MTBC positive, bacteriologically confirmed TB = MTB+ve/Rif-ve |
| Reflex Xpert MTB/XDR Assay should be done to rule out INH and fluoroquinolone resistance. |
| Facilities with Xpert MTB/XDR onsite are to initiate treatment after receiving Xpert MTB/XDR assay results. |
| Start first-line anti-TB treatment for MTB +ve/Rif -ve while waiting for Xpert MTB/XDR and DST results if not available onsite |
| All Xpert positive (MTB +ve/Rif-ve) cases must have reflex MGIT culture and DST done on a second sample at the time of diagnosis |
| Xpert MTB-positive patients should be monitored while on treatment using smear microscopy at the recommended intervals until completion of treatment. |
| Note: Xpert MTB/RIF® Ultra can detect dead bacilli so culture confirmation is needed for previously treated cases. Awaiting culture, should not delay initiation of TB treatment but treatment should be based on the clinical condition of the patient. If in doubt, it is also important to consult a Medical Officer. |
| MTB was detected, and Rifampicin resistance detected |
| (All patients whose diagnosis of TB has been confirmed by Xpert MTB/RIF® Ultra with evidence of Rifampicin resistance) |
| Should be registered as Rifampicin-resistant (RR-TB) cases = MTB +ve/Rif +ve. |
| RR-TB diagnosis is considered a proxy for MDR-TB; and should therefore be started on a DR-TB treatment regimen according to the DR-TB management chapter. |
| All Xpert diagnosed RR-TB positive (MTB +ve/Rif +ve) cases must have reflex Xpert MTB/XDR Assay to determine INH and fluoroquinolone resistance. |
| Targeted genome sequencing, MGIT culture and phenotypic DST should be done on the second sample at the time of diagnosis. |
| Xpert-diagnosed RR-TB patients should be monitored by sputum smear microscopy and MGIT culture as per the National TB management guidelines. |

Assess: TB signs and symptoms†; whether seriously ill*; advanced HIV disease (AHD)**; perform CD4 testing (if eligible); perform CXR/CRP screening if eligible and available†.

Results of Xpert and LAM: both negative → clinical management, provide TPT if eligible; Xpert AND/OR LAM positive → start TB treatment and perform work-up to exclude DR-TB (collect a specimen for phenotypic and genotypic DST).

text:
### 4.5.1 Role of plain chest radiography (Chest X-ray) (Chest X-rays are not necessary for the routine follow-up of a patient on TB treatment but can be used for exceptional cases such as EPTB and in childr)

| Chest X-rays are not necessary for the routine follow-up of a patient on TB treatment but can be used for exceptional cases such as EPTB and in children. |
| --- |
| They are not required to change to continuation phase or to stop treatment in patients who are clinically responding well to TB therapy. |
| Chest x-rays are contra-indicated in pregnancy especially during the first trimester. If absolutely required, it is to be taken with protective LED-shield. |

heading_path: Chapter 4: TB and Drug-Resistant TB Diagnosis > Table 11: A brief details of type of EP-TB, clinical features and diagnostic procedure
text:
### Table 11: A brief details of type of EP-TB, clinical features and diagnostic procedure (Type of EPTB, Clinical Features, Diagnosis) Table 11: A brief details of type of EP-TB, clinical features and diagnostic procedure | Type of EPTB | Clinical Features | Diagnosis | | --- | --- | --- | | TB Lymphadenitis (most common EPTB site) | Fever, weight loss, fatigue and occasionally night sweat or no symptoms at all.

Enlarged lymph nodes (>2cm). They can break down due to the formation of caseous pus. Cervical LN is the most common.

Mediastinal or abdominal LNs, if large may obstruct nearby 'hollow' organs producing such symptoms as stridor, dysphagia, intestinal obstruction, etc. | \* Fine needle aspiration of the LN and send the specimen for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra® and Xpert MTB/XDR testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable. | | Pleural TB (Extra-pulmonary TB) | Acute or sub-acute illness varies from a few days to a few weeks.

Pleuritic chest pains, non-productive cough and dyspnoea, sometimes fever.

In an empyema complicated pleural TB, the patient may be acutely ill with chest pains, breathlessness, and cough with expectoration, fever and toxaemia. Occasionally it may be present as a chest wall mass or draining sinus tract. | - By therapeutic/diagnostic tap and sending the fluid for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra® and Xpert MTB/XDR testing and culture / DST and tNGS where applicable. | | TB Meningitis | Meningism (neck stiffness, Kerning's sign), irritability, anorexia, vomiting, fever and sometimes seizures.

Complete or partial loss of vision is a major complication of TBM.

Without treatment the patient may descend into a coma and death would follow in five to eight weeks. Thus, patients need immediate admission. | Lumbar puncture for CSF examination: increased lymphocytes, increased proteins and decreased glucose. | | Abdominal TB | Symptoms are non-specific and depend on the organs involved and extent of the disease.

Loss of appetite, malaise, diarrhea, low grade fever, weight loss, night sweats, ascites, masses or abscess, obstructive jaundice, etc. | • Diagnostic/therapeutic tap for ascites and send for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra® and Xpert MTB/XDR testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable. | | Pericardial TB | Fever, weakness, cough, vague chest pains, dyspnoea, weight loss and swollen feet.

On examination there may be muffled heart sounds, pericardial rub, elevated jugular venous pressure, and signs of right-sided ventricular failure. | • Clinical diagnosis, cardiomegaly on the chest X-ray and echocardiogram.

• In case pericardiocentesis is performed, the liquid should be sent for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and Xpert MTB/XDR® testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable. | | TB of the bones and joints | Spinal TB (Potts disease) is the most common, usually, constitutional symptoms (weakness, loss of appetite and weight, night sweats) will be present before any signs of spinal involvement (chronic back pain and gibbous deformity). If untreated, patients can develop neurological deficits and paraplegia.

TB of the joints affects the movement of the affected joints and produces pain. | • Spinal X-ray will show paravertebral soft tissue shadowing, vertebral collapse and loss of intervertebral disc space.

• These patients need to be referred to a specialist for treatment. | | Miliary TB | This is disseminated TB and patients are usually very ill with signs of systemic toxaemia: fever, circulatory collapse and tachycardia.

There may be cough, meningism and hepatosplenomegaly. | • Chest X-ray: diffuse miliary nodules.

• Sputum samples for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and MTB XDR Assay® testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable.

• CSF, liver biopsy and bone marrow biopsy may reveal evidence of TB. |

Abdominal TBSymptoms are non-specific and depend on the organs involved and extent of the disease.<br/><br/>Loss of appetite, malaise, diarrhea, low grade fever, weight loss, night sweats, ascites, masses or abscess, obstructive jaundice, etc.• Diagnostic/therapeutic tap for ascites and send for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra® and Xpert MTB/XDR testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable.
Pericardial TBFever, weakness, cough, vague chest pains, dyspnoea, weight loss and swollen feet.<br/><br/>On examination there may be muffled heart sounds, pericardial rub, elevated jugular venous pressure, and signs of right-sided ventricular failure.• Clinical diagnosis, cardiomegaly on the chest X-ray and echocardiogram.<br/><br/>• In case pericardiocentesis is performed, the liquid should be sent for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and Xpert MTB/XDR® testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable.
TB of the bones and jointsSpinal TB (Potts disease) is the most common, usually, constitutional symptoms (weakness, loss of appetite and weight, night sweats) will be present before any signs of spinal involvement (chronic back pain and gibbous deformity). If untreated, patients can develop neurological deficits and paraplegia.<br/><br/>TB of the joints affects the movement of the affected joints and produces pain.• Spinal X-ray will show paravertebral soft tissue shadowing, vertebral collapse and loss of intervertebral disc space.<br/><br/>• These patients need to be referred to a specialist for treatment.
Miliary TBThis is disseminated TB and patients are usually very ill with signs of systemic toxaemia: fever, circulatory collapse and tachycardia.<br/><br/>There may be cough, meningism and hepatosplenomegaly.• Chest X-ray: diffuse miliary nodules.<br/><br/>• Sputum samples for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and MTB XDR Assay® testing and culture/DST, and tNGS where applicable.<br/><br/>• CSF, liver biopsy and bone marrow biopsy may reveal evidence of TB.

heading_path: 5.3 Disposal of Laboratory Materials
text:
### 5.3 Disposal of Laboratory Materials (Description)

5.3 Disposal of Laboratory Materials TB Specimens examined in the laboratory are potentially infectious. Hence, after examination, they must be disinfected and destroyed so that the risk of infection is reduced. All disposable containers must be used only once. Sputum cups which contain sputum can be disposed of by any one of the following methods:

|  | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Disinfection | After the TB specimens have been used, all sputum cups should be kept in a bucket containing 5% hypochlorite, 10% bleach solution (freshly prepared), or 5% phenol solution. The caps of the sputum cups must be removed and the cups, caps and wooden sticks completely submerged in the solution in a secure place for at least 18 hours. After this, the solution, cups, caps and wooden sticks can be discarded with other hospital waste. This bin/bucket should have a lid which is foot operated. |
| Incineration | Wherever incinerators exist, the type specified under the Biomedical Waste Management & Handling Rules of the country, with a combustion efficiency of 99%, should be used. Sputum cups made of polypropylene should be used wherever available. (Note: If sputum cups are made of other varieties of plastic, they should be disinfected and destroyed as per the hospital waste management rules). Burning is NOT recommended. |
| Autoclaving | The sputum cups and lids, with the lids removed, along with wooden sticks can be autoclaved at the end of each day's laboratory work. The autoclave cycle should have a holding time of 15 minutes at 121°C HTAT (Holding time at temperature), 10 minutes at 126°C HTAT or 3 minutes at 134°C HTAT. The material can be discarded with other waste after proper cooling. |

heading_path: 6.7 The Role of Adjuvant Steroid Treatment > Table 16: Steroid indication and recommended doses in TB management
text:
### Table 16: Steroid indication and recommended doses in TB management (Indication, Prednisolone treatment (dose for children in brackets), Dexamethasone treatment)

Adjuvant steroids are recommended for TB meningitis (decreased consciousness, neurological defects or spinal block) and TB pericarditis (with effusion or constriction); from expert opinion also for large symptomatic pleural effusion, hypoadrenalism, TB laryngitis with airway obstruction, severe hypersensitivity reactions to TB drugs, renal tract TB and massive lymph node enlargement with pressure effects. Rifampicin reduces the bioavailability of prednisolone.

| Indication | Prednisolone treatment (dose for children in brackets) | Dexamethasone treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TB meningitis | 60 mg (1–2 mg/kg) daily for weeks 1–4, then decrease over several weeks | Intravenous dexamethasone for 4 weeks (0.4 mg/kg per day in week 1, 0.3 mg/kg per day in week 2, 0.2 mg/kg per day in week 3 and 0.1 mg/kg per day in week 4), followed by a taper of oral dexamethasone (4 mg/day, 3 mg/day, 2 mg/day and 1 mg/day, each for 1 week). |
| TB pericarditis | 60 mg (1–2 mg/kg) daily for weeks 1–4; 30 mg (0.5–1 mg/kg) daily for weeks 5–8; then decrease over several weeks | — |
| TB pleural effusion | 30 mg (0.5–1 mg/kg) daily for 1–2 weeks | — |

Source: TB/HIV. A Clinical Manual, WHO/HTM/TB/2006.420.

text:
### Table 19: Definition of TB treatment outcomes (Outcome, Definition) Table 19: Definition of TB treatment outcomes | Outcome | Definition | | --- | --- | | Cured | A bacteriologically confirmed case, who is smear or culture-negative in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion (at least 7 days apart)a | | Treatment completed | A patient who completed treatment but who does not have a negative sputum smear or culture result in the last month of treatment and in at least one previous occasionb | | Treatment Failure | ● A patient whose sputum culture is positive at 2 months, or smear is positive at 5 months or later during treatment.
● Clinically diagnosed PTB or extra-pulmonary TB patients with clinical condition not improving or worsening (clinically judged)
● Patients found to harbour a DR strain at any time during the treatment (excluding baseline sample) | | Died | A patient who dies for any reason during the course of treatment | | Loss to follow-up | A patient whose treatment was interrupted for 2 or more consecutive months | | Not evaluated | Patient for whom no treatment outcome is assigned; Include former “transfer-out” in this category | | Treatment successc | The sum of cured and completed treatment | | (a) These definitions apply to bacteriologically confirmed and clinically diagnosed pulmonary TB patients, and patients with extra-pulmonary disease. (b) The sputum examination may not have been done, or the results may not be available (c) For all patients, bacteriologically confirmed and clinically diagnosed pulmonary TB patients, and extra-pulmonary TB patients. | |

source_flags: Treatment failure is defined as 'sputum culture positive at 2 months, or smear positive at 5 months or later'. In the WHO definitions failure is a positive smear/culture at month 5 or later (or treatment change); a positive culture at month 2 is not treatment failure.

heading_path: 7.3 Treatment of DR-TB > 7.3.5 DRTB Treatment in Comorbidities and Special Situations > 7.3.5.4 People with renal disease > Table 26: Recommended Dosing of TB Drugs for Patients with Renal Failure
text:
### Table 26: Recommended Dosing of TB Drugs for Patients with Renal Failure (Drug, Recommended dose and frequency for patients with CrCl < 30 ml/min or receiving hemodialysis)

Renal disease is not an absolute contraindication to BPaLM; use clinical judgement and monitor renal function. If a regimen other than BPaLM is used, adjust doses for the degree of renal failure (CrCl < 30 ml/min).

| Drug | Recommended dose and frequency for patients with CrCl < 30 ml/min or receiving haemodialysis |
| --- | --- |
| Pyrazinamide | 25 – 35 mg/kg per dose three times per week (not daily) |
| Ethambutol | 15 – 25 mg/kg per dose three times per week (not daily) |
| Amikacin | 12 – 15 mg/kg per dose two or three times per week (not daily) |
| Levofloxacin | 750 – 1000 mg per dose three times per week (not daily) |
| Cycloserine | 250 mg once daily, or 500 mg/dose three times per week |
| Amoxicillin/clavulanate | CrCl 10 – 30 ml/min: 1000 mg as amoxicillin component BID; CrCl < 10 ml/min: 1000 mg as amoxicillin component OD |
| Imipenem/cilastatin | CrCl 20 – 40 ml/min: 500 mg every 8 hours; CrCl < 20 ml/min: 500 mg every 12 hours |
| Meropenem | CrCl 20 – 40 ml/min: 750 mg every 12 hours; CrCl < 20 ml/min: 500 mg every 12 hours |

source_flags: Linezolid alternative: '300 mg daily provided that 9 consecutive weeks of treatment is completed' is ambiguous; in the WHO BPaLM guidance linezolid 600 mg daily may be reduced to 300 mg daily after the first 9 weeks (or for toxicity); a three-times-weekly 600 mg schedule is not part of the WHO recommendation.
The total bedaquiline course (weeks 3-24/26 at 200 mg three times weekly) and the BPaLM duration (6 months) are not stated in the table.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Childhood TB Screening, Diagnosis and Treatment > 8.3 Diagnosis of Childhood TB > Table 32: Procedures of respiratory sample and stool sample collection
text:
### Table 32: Procedures of respiratory sample and stool sample collection (Method, Techniques) | Method | Techniques | | --- | --- | | Sputum Induction | | | Gastric Aspirate | • Consider in children < 7 years
• Nasogastric aspiration of gastric secretions using a nasogastric tube
• 2-3 specimens are recommended to increase yield
• Volume: 5-10 ml should be collected, if less confirm tube placement and re-attempt. If still < 5-10 ml instill up to 20 ml of sterile water and re-aspirate.
• It should be performed in the early morning and fast for 4 hours (outpatient collection is fine provided these parameters are met).
• Nasogastric tube should be used
• If possible, neutralize the aspirate with sodium bicarbonate if the specimen is not processed that day based on pH testing | | Nasopharyngeal Aspirate | • Can be performed in children under 6 years
• Suctioning of the nasopharynx via a nasopharyngeal tube at 15 -20 kPa of pressure
• 2 ml of aspirate is recommended
• Can be performed at any time but morning is preferred, generally follows sputum induction
• A suction machine is recommended for the procedure | | Stool for TB | • Performed only for children under the age of 15 years.
• For infants and toddlers, stools can be directly collected from the diaper as soon as possible after defecation. (Avoiding prolonged contact with the surface of the diaper.)
• Older children are directed to defecate on a clean sheet of paper, avoiding contamination from the soil and urine.
• Using a designated spatula or wooden stick, the sample is transferred into a stool container or a sputum container and sealed tightly before submitting it to the laboratory for processing. The sample container should NOT be filled to the brim.
• A volume of 1g (a pea size) for a formed stool or 5 ml for a watery stool is sufficient to perform the Xpert test.
• The simple one-step method (SOS) is used in the laboratory to analyse the sample.
• A subsequently induced sputum or gastric aspirate will have to be collected and sent for culture and DST to the reference lab should the Xpert MTB results turn out positive. | | Methods of specimen collection for Extra-Pulmonary Disease | • Specimen collection should be attempted from the presumed site of disease through fine needle aspiration of lymph nodes, collection of CSFS, pleural, ascetic fluid etc. |

### Table 33: Danger and Priority Signs in Children <10 Years Old (Age <5 yrs, Age <5-9 yrs, Age <10 yrs) Table 33: Danger and Priority Signs in Children <10 Years Old | Age <5 yrs | Age <5-9 yrs | Age <10 yrs | | --- | --- | --- | | Danger Signs (IMCI) | Danger Signs (ETAT) | Priority Signs | | Gastrointestinal/circulatory:
• Unable to eat or drink
• Vomiting up everything
• Signs of severe dehydration (sunken eyes, skin pinch returns very slowly)
• Severe palmar pallor | Gastrointestinal/circulatory:
• Diarrhea with any two signs of severe dehydration (lethargy, unconsciousness, sunken eyes, very slow return of skin after pinching)
• Signs of shock (cold extremities with capillary refill time>3 seconds, weak and fast pulse) | Any sick child aged <2 months
• High fever (>39° C)
• Severe pallor
• Respiratory distress
• Restless, continuously irritable, lethargic
• Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) | | Respiratory:
• Stridor
• Oxygen saturation <90% | Respiratory:
• Obstructed or absent
• Breathing
• Severe respiratory distress
• Central cyanosis | | | Neurological:
• Seizures

heading_path: Chapter 8: Childhood TB Screening, Diagnosis and Treatment > Table 38: Recommended dosing for 6RHZ+Ethionamide regimen for TB meningitis in children and adolescents
text:
### Table 38: Recommended dosing for 6RHZ+Ethionamide regimen for TB meningitis in children and adolescents (Drug, Dosage (mg/kg))

Short 6-month TBM regimen (6RHZ+Ethionamide), recommended by WHO (2022) for children and adolescents 0-19 years as an alternative to 2HRZE/10HR; all drugs given daily for 6 months. Not recommended for children and adolescents living with HIV (use the 12-month regimen).

| Drug | Dosage (mg/kg) | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Isoniazid (H) | 15-20 | Higher end of dosing for younger children and lower end for older children. |
| Rifampicin (R) | 22.5-30 | Higher end of dosing for younger children and lower end for older children. |
| Pyrazinamide (Z) | 35-45 | Higher end of dosing for younger children and lower end for older children. |
| Ethionamide (Eto) | 17.5-22.5 | Higher end of dosing for younger children and lower end for older children. |

**Note:** The alternative regimen for TB meningitis in children is 2HRZE+Lfx/10RH with an increased dose of rifampicin (25-30 mg/kg) as per the BMC trial; this regimen is not yet recommended by WHO. Boxed recommendation printed below the table: 'Recommended TBM regimen for children: 2HRZE+Lfx / 10RH (increase the dose of rifampicin to 25 - 30 mg/kg).'

heading_path: Chapter 8: Childhood TB Screening, Diagnosis and Treatment > TB Screening Algorithms for Children > Figure 23: Children <15 Years at Health Facilities
text:
### Figure 23. TB screening algorithm for children <15 years at health facilities: symptom screen by age, risk factors (TB contact, MUAC, vulnerable children), CXR by human reader, sputum or stool Xpert, LF-LAM for children with HIV, TPT

Population: children and adolescents <15 years attending health facilities.
1. Symptom screen: for 10–15 years, current cough OR fever OR weight loss OR night sweats (W4SS); for <10 years, cough, fever, weight loss/poor weight gain of any duration, or history of TB contact.
   - Positive: collect two specimens (if <5 years or cannot produce sputum, collect one stool sample) and perform microbiological assessment for active TB (including LF-LAM for children living with HIV*).
   - Negative: assess risk factors – child TB contact, nutrition status (MUAC <12.5 cm for <5 years, <22.5 cm for >5 years), vulnerable children (e.g. orphans).
     - No risk factors: exit.
     - Risk factors: was CXR screening done in the past 12 months? Yes: further clinical evaluation, provide TPT if eligible. No: CXR read by a human reader → suggestive of TB: collect specimens as above; negative: further clinical evaluation, TPT if eligible; non-TB abnormalities: clinical assessment for active TB if symptoms persist or other morbidity, take CXR if not taken before, provide TPT if eligible.
2. Microbiological result: positive → initiate TB treatment; negative → clinical assessment for active TB if symptoms persist or other morbidity, take CXR if not taken before, provide TPT if eligible.
* Perform TB-LAM for all with AHD (CD4 <200, WHO stage 3 or 4) regardless of symptoms, seriously ill regardless of CD4, and all presumptive TB regardless of CD4.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Childhood TB Screening, Diagnosis and Treatment > TB Screening Algorithms for Children > Figure 24: Children <15 Years (With and Without HIV) at Facilities with X-ray, CAD/AI and CRP
text:
### Figure 24. TB screening algorithm for children <15 years with and without HIV at facilities with X-ray, CAD/AI and CRP: symptom screen, risk factors, ART status, CRP (>10 years), CXR by human reader, sputum/stool Xpert, TB-LAM, TPT

Population: children and adolescents <15 years attending health facilities (non-PLHIV and PLHIV).
1. Symptom screen: current cough OR fever OR weight loss (poor weight gain, failure to thrive) OR night sweats.
   - Positive (with or without HIV): collect two sputum samples (if <5 years or cannot produce sputum, one stool sample) and perform microbiological assessment for active TB (including TB-LAM for eligible PLHIV**).

2. Microbiological result: positive → initiate active TB treatment; negative → further clinical evaluation, provide TPT if eligible.

heading_path: 9.4 Monitoring of TB Patients for Adverse Effects of Anti-TB Drugs > Pharmacovigilance and Adverse Event Management > Table 39: Guide to management of side effects of first line
text:
### Table 39: Guide to management of side effects of first line (Side effects, Drugs (probably responsible), Management)

Table 39: Guide to management of side effects of first line Source: Treatment of tuberculosis guidelines. 5thEdition. WHO/HTM/TB/2017

| Side effects | Drugs (probably responsible) | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Major |  |  |
| Generalized severe skin rash with or without itching | Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol | Stop anti-TB drugs and refer. Re-challenge once stable, starting with the least likely causative agent. Give antihistamines to manage pruritis |
| Deafness (no wax on otoscopy) | Injectable \* | Stop Injectable and refer |
| Dizziness (vertigo and nystagmus) | Injectable \* | Stop Injectable and refer |
| Jaundice (other causes excluded), hepatitis | Pyrazinamide, INH, Rifampicin | Stop anti-TB drugs and refer Re-challenge once stable starting with the least hepatotoxic agent |
| Confusion (suspect drug-induced acute liver failure if there is jaundice) | Most anti-TB drugs | Stop anti-TB drugs and refer |
| Visual impairment (other causes excluded) | Ethambutol | Stop Ethambutol and refer |
| Shock, purpura, acute renal failure | Rifampicin | Stop Rifampicin and refer |
| Decreased urine output (acute renal failure) | Injectable \* | Stop Injectable and refer Adjust the doses of other renally-excreted drugs e.g. Ethambutol |
| Minor |  |  |
| Anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain | Pyrazinamide, Rifampicin, INH | Give drugs with small meals or just before bedtime and advise the patient to swallow pills slowly with small sips of water. If the symptoms persist or worsen, or there is protracted vomiting or any sign of bleeding, consider the side-effect to be major and refer to the Clinician urgently. |
| Joint pains | Pyrazinamide | Aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or Paracetamol. |
| Major |  |  |
| Burning, numbness or tingling sensation in the hands or feet | INH | Give Pyridoxine 50-75mg daily Can go up to 100mg. Refer if no improvement or grade 3 or 4 neuropathy. |
| Drowsiness | INH | Reassure the patient. Give drugs before bedtime. |
| Orange/red urine | Rifampicin | Reassure patient. Patients should be informed about the urine change when initiating TB treatment. |
| Flu-like syndrome (fever, chills, malaise, headache, bone pain) | Intermittent dosing of Rifampicin | Reassure patient. When starting TB treatment, patients should be informed about the possibility of such occurring and that it is normal. |

text:
### Table 43: Blood Potassium levels and recommended monitoring protocol (Potassium level mEq/L, Quantity of KCL 1mEq I. V=1mmol I.V 8mEq=600mg tablet, When to do the next control (sooner if the patient has vomiting or diarr)

| Potassium level (mEq/L) | Quantity of KCl (1 mEq IV = 1 mmol IV; 8 mEq = 600 mg tablet) | When to do the next control (sooner if the patient has vomiting or diarrhoea) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4.0 or more | None | Monthly |
| 3.7 – 4.0 | None | Monthly |
| 3.4 – 3.6 | 20 - 40 mEq (1500-3000 mg) | Monthly |
| 3.0 – 3.3 | 60 mEq (4500 mg) | Two weeks |
| 2.7 – 2.9 | 80 mEq (6000 mg) | One week |
| 2.4 – 2.6 | 60 mmol IV and 6000 mg orally every 6 hours for 24 hours | — |
| 2.0 – 2.3 | 60 mmol IV and 7500 mg orally | Every 6 hours with aggressive IV replacement. Consider holding the injectable until >2.4 |

**Note:** Every Slow-K 600 mg tablet contains 8 mEq of K; every magnesium tablet contains 150 mg magnesium oxide. Potassium IV supplementation should NOT exceed 20 mmol/hr of KCl (usual 40 mmol in 1 L NaCl 0.9%, maximum 60 mmol/L). Magnesium IV: maximum 5 g MgSO4 in 1 L NaCl 0.9% or dextrose 5%, not faster than 150 mg/min; if not an emergency 2 g in 100 ml over 1-2 hours or 4 g in 250 ml over 2-4 hours. Amiloride or spironolactone are useful in resistant cases.

Source: Guidelines for Programmatic Management of Drug-resistant Tuberculosis, Emergency update 2008, WHO/HTM/TB/2008.402.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Pharmacovigilance and Adverse Event Management > 9.9 Algorithms for Management of Adverse Events with Second-line Anti-TB Drugs > Figure 28: Management of QTc Prolongation
text:
### Figure 28. Management of QTcF prolongation on second-line TB drugs (BDQ, CFZ, MFX, DLM, LFX): ECG monitoring, grades 1-4 and actions, order of stopping drugs

Items: If on multiple QtcF prolonging drugs, stop ancillary drugs first. Then stop MFX if receiving this drug. If QTcF prolongation persists, then stop CFZ. If CTcF prolongation persists, then stop BDQ.
- Causative Medications: BDQ, CFZ, MFX, DLM, LFX -> QTcF prolongation: Signs and symptoms include palpitations, syncope/fainting, dizziness
- Monitor for QTcF prolongation by checking an ECG at baseline, week 2 and monthly until month 6 or anytime if there are symptoms -> QTcF prolongation: Signs and symptoms include palpitations, syncope/fainting, dizziness
- QTcF prolongation: Signs and symptoms include palpitations, syncope/fainting, dizziness -> Assess ECG. If QtcF is prolonged, repeat ECG. Consider other possible causes including low potassium, malnutrition, hypothyroidism or other medications. Consider checking and replacing potassium if vomiting or diarrhea.
- Assess ECG. If QtcF is prolonged, repeat ECG. Consider other possible causes including low potassium, malnutrition, hypothyroidism or other medications. Consider checking and replacing potassium if vomiting or diarrhea. -> Assess severity and manage
- Assess severity and manage -> Mild/Grade 1: *45 - 480 msec* Monitor closely, weekly ECG until QTcF < grade or baseline; correct electrolytes or other causes as needed; Moderate/Grade 2: *> 480 - 500 msec* Monitor closely, weekly ECG until QTcF < grade or baseline; correct electrolytes or other causes as needed; Severe/Grade 3: *> 500 msec* Stop the suspected causative drug(s); hospitalize and correct electrolytes or other underlying causes as needed; Life-threatening/Grade 4: *> 501 msec or 60 msec change from baseline and one of the following:* Torsades de pointers polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, or signs/symptoms or serious arrhythmia. Stop the suspected causative drugs; hospitalize and correct electrolytes or other underlying causes

text:

heading_path: Chapter 9: Pharmacovigilance and Adverse Event Management > 9.9 Algorithms for Management of Adverse Events with Second-line Anti-TB Drugs > Figure 31: Management of Liver Function Abnormalities
text:
### Figure 31. Management of liver function abnormalities on TB drugs (PZA, INH, BDQ, CFZ, Eto, PAS): LFT monitoring, grades 1-4 by ULN, stop and reintroduce drugs, liver-sparing regimen

- Causative Medications: PZA, INH, BDQ, CFZ, Eto, PAS -> Liver Function Abnormalities: Liver function test abnormalities can present asymptomaticaly or with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice/icterus, itching
- Monitor elevated liver function tests at baseline and monthly for the first six months of treatment and anytime if there are symptoms -> Liver Function Abnormalities: Liver function test abnormalities can present asymptomaticaly or with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice/icterus, itching
- Liver Function Abnormalities: Liver function test abnormalities can present asymptomaticaly or with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice/icterus, itching -> Assess for other causes. These include alcohol use, use of traditional medicines/ herbs, viral hepatitis and TB itself
- Assess for other causes. These include alcohol use, use of traditional medicines/ herbs, viral hepatitis and TB itself -> Assess severity and manage
- Assess severity and manage -> Mild/Grade 1: >1 to 2.5 times ULN and asymptomatic Continue treatment and follow until return to baseline or stabilization of AST/ALT elevation; Moderate/Grade 2: >2.5 to 5 times ULN and asymptomatic Continue treatment and follow until return to baseline or stabilization of AST/ALT elevation; Severe/Grade 3: > 5 to 10 ULN or any asymptomatic elevations Stop all drugs, measure LFTs weekly; reintroduce drugs after toxicity is resolved; Life-threatening/Grade 4: > 10 time ULN regardless of symptoms Stop all drugs, measure LFTs weekly; reintroduce drugs after toxicity is resolved
Liver-sparing regimen drugs: EMB, DLM, CS, amikacin (with caution) and likely the FQs. People with underlying liver disease, heavy alcohol use or viral hepatitis should start a modified shorter regimen that includes CS and does NOT include INH or PZA.

heading_path: 10.1 TB/HIV interaction and the comprehensive package of care > 10.1.5 When to start ART? > Table 45: Recommended periods to start ART in PLHIV with presumptive TB and confirmed TB
text:
### Table 45: Recommended periods to start ART in PLHIV with presumptive TB and confirmed TB (Patient Category, When to start ART)

Table 45: Recommended periods to start ART in PLHIV with presumptive TB and confirmed TB

| Patient Category | When to start ART |
| --- | --- |
| Among PLHIV who are presumptive for TB | Initiate ART while rapidly investigating for TB, with close follow-up within seven days to initiate TB treatment if TB is confirmed |
| Among PLHIV on ART and diagnosed with TB | Continue ART and initiate anti-TB treatment as soon as diagnosed, may need to adjust ART regimen/dosage if required |
| For newly diagnosed PLHIV/returnees who also have been diagnosed with TB | Initiate ART as soon as possible preferably within 2 weeks of initiating tuberculosis treatment (including same-day anti-TB and ART treatment if clinically stable) regardless of immune status |
| Patients with TB meningitis | Delay ART to 4 weeks post-initiation of anti-TB treatment |

heading_path: 10.1 TB/HIV interaction and the comprehensive package of care > 10.1.6 What ART regimen to start on? > Table 46: Recommended Adult ART Regimens for TB/HIV Co-infected patients
text:
### Table 46: Recommended Adult ART Regimens for TB/HIV Co-infected patients (Client Category, Recommended ART regimen, Comments) | Client category | Recommended ART regimen | Comments | | --- | --- | --- | | Clients already on TB treatment presenting for ART initiation | TDF (300 mg)/3TC (300 mg) once daily + DTG (50 mg twice daily) | - Start ART as soon as possible with increased DTG dosing of 50 mg twice daily
- Return to standard DTG dosing 50 mg once daily two weeks after the completion of TB treatment | | Clients developing TB while on a DTG-based ART regimen | Increase DTG dose to 50 mg twice daily | Clients must return to DTG 50 mg once daily 2 weeks after completing TB treatment. | | Developing DS-TB while on an EFV-based ART regimen | TDF/3TC+EFV 400 mg (once daily) | - Check VL at the end of treatment. If VL is undetectable, the client can be transitioned to a once-daily FDC of TDF+3TC+DTG two weeks after completion of TB treatment
- If VL is detectable, immediately switch to second line and continue adherence support (refer to the ART section) | | Developing DS-TB while on a protease inhibitor (PI)-based ART regimen | Consult an experienced HIV clinician or snapthirdline@mohcoag.org before choosing these options:
TB patient on LPV/r:
- Super-boost LPV/r to 400 mg/400 mg by adding 300 mg ritonavir, and continue until 2 weeks after completion of TB treatment
- Double-dose LPV/r to 800 mg/200 mg twice daily (double dosing is only for clients >10 years of age) and continue until 2 weeks after completion of TB treatment
- If evidence of VL suppression in the past 3-6 months, switch to a DTG-based second-line regimen and continue twice-daily DTG until 2 weeks after completion of TB treatment
TB patient on ATV/r or DRV/r:
- Do not combine with rifampicin
- Change to DTG twice daily if DTG-naive, or LPV/r with adjustments as above if DTG-experienced
Patients who may be failing ART:
- Follow guidance on managing treatment failure | (same as left) | **For clients with multidrug-resistant TB** | Client category | Recommended ART regimen | Comments | | --- | --- | --- | | EFV and bedaquiline (BDQ) | - EFV should not be used with BDQ.
- EFV induces CYP3A activity and co-administration with BDQ may result in reduced BDQ exposure and loss of BDQ activity.
- DTG is the preferred INSTI for clients receiving BDQ. | (same as left) | | Delamanid (DLM) and ARVs | - DLM is generally considered safe to administer with ART.
- Evidence shows safety with EFV, TDF and LPV/r.
- No LPV/r dose adjustment is needed for TB patients on DLM. No long-term studies have been done on drug-drug interactions between DLM and ARVs. DTG is the preferred INSTI for clients receiving DLM. | (same as left) | **Note:** For all clients, maintain the same NRTI backbone provided no dose adjustment is necessary and the client is virally suppressed.

For clients with multidrug-resistant TB

### Table 47: TB treatment/ART Drug Interactions (Drug combination, Considerations)

Table 47: TB treatment/ART Drug Interactions

| Drug combination | Considerations |
| --- | --- |
| Rifampicin and (LPV/r) | - LPV/r can be used with Rifampicin - Super boost the LPV/r (1:1 lopinavir and ritonavir) by adding ritonavir. - Closely monitor the client for toxicity (especially gastrointestinal intolerance) and virological failure |
| Rifampicin and Oral Contraceptive Pill | - Oral contraceptive pills may not be effective when administered with RIF. - Women of childbearing age should either receive a contraceptive pill containing a higher dose of oestrogen (50μg) or use another form of contraception (e.g., medroxyprogesterone). - Emphasize concomitant condom use during this period |

If the VL is detectable, immediately switch to the second line and continue adherence support. - If the client is on a DTG regimen, the DTG does need to be given as 50mg twice daily until at least 2 weeks after the client has completed TB treatment. This may increase the occurrence of DTG side effects. |

### Table 50: TB/HIV Simplified Treatment Table (Treatment of HIV-associated TB in children)

**Treatment of HIV-associated TB in children – patients initiating ART while on TB treatment**

| Weight | Current ART regimen | Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| < 10 kg | Not on ART | LPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ¹ ⁶ (recommended) or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³ (recommended if ritonavir is not available) or NVP ² ³ ⁴ ⁵ |
| 10-20 kg | Not on ART | EFV (recommended) or LPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ¹ ⁶ or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³ |
| > 20 kg | Not on ART | DTG ⁷ twice daily (recommended) |

**Modifications to ART when initiating TB treatment in patients on ART**

| Weight | Current ART regimen | Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| < 10 kg | NVP | Continue NVP ² ³ ⁴ ⁵ |
| < 10 kg | LPV/r | LPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ¹ ⁶ (recommended) or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³ (recommended if ritonavir not available) or NVP ² ³ ⁴ ⁵ |
| 10-20 kg | NVP or EFV | EFV ⁸ |
| 10-20 kg | LPV/r (1st-line ART) | LPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ¹ ⁶ (recommended) or EFV (recommended if VL undetectable in the last 6 months) or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³ |
| 10-20 kg | LPV/r (2nd-line treatment) | LPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ⁶ (recommended) or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³ |
| > 20 kg | NVP or EFV | EFV ⁸ ⁹ |
| > 20 kg | ATV/r or LPV/r (1st or 2nd line) | LPV/r double dose ⁶ or DTG ⁷ twice daily (if VL confirmed undetectable at TB treatment initiation) |
| > 20 kg | DTG | Twice-daily DTG ⁷ |

**Note:** Guiding principles: always immediately check viral load and CD4 in a patient on ART who is diagnosed with TB; if VL is detectable avoid a one-drug change and manage as treatment failure considering ART/ATT interactions; consider ART and PMTCT history; NRTI companion drugs per HIV guidelines (weight, comorbidities, prior NRTI exposure); consult TB/HIV experts (NTCP, ENAP, partners) for questions and patients failing second-line ART or a PI.

1. See Dosing Table **** for 1:1 LPV/r (ritonavir solution and capsules) [as printed]. 2. NEVER continue ABC-3TC-AZT or an NVP-based regimen for more than 2 weeks after rifampicin is discontinued. 3. Consider ABC-3TC-AZT or NVP if intolerant to LPV/r. 4. Avoid NVP if prior exposure to PMTCT or ART. 5. Start at full dose and increase the dose to 200 mg/m²/dose if formulation allows when co-administered with rifampicin. 6. LPV/r can be administered as a double dose instead of 1:1 in children swallowing LPV/r tablets, reduced to standard dosing 2 weeks after rifampicin is discontinued. 7. DTG must be given twice daily while on TB treatment and continued twice daily for two weeks after rifampicin is discontinued. 8. NVP can be continued during TB treatment instead of EFV if intolerance or cannot swallow EFV. 9. Plan to change to DTG from EFV following completion of TB treatment (two weeks after rifampicin is stopped) if viral load is undetectable.

heading_path: Chapter 11: TB Preventive Treatment > 11.6 Ruling out Active TB Disease > Figure 35: HIV-negative Household Contacts >10 Years and Other Risk Groups
text:
### Figure 35. Ruling out active TB before TPT in HIV-negative household contacts >10 years and other risk groups: symptom screen/CXR, TB infection test, start TPT

- Household TB contacts. Other Risk Groups* -> Symptom based screening (CXR if available)
- Symptom based screening (CXR if available) -> Positive (S/S and/or CXC); *Negative (S/S and/or CXC)
- Positive (S/S and/or CXC) -> Evaluate for TB/DR-TB
- Evaluate for TB/DR-TB -> TB/DR-TB disease; No TB
- TB/DR-TB disease -> Treat for TB/DR-TB
- No TB -> Start TPT
- *Negative (S/S and/or CXC) -> Perform TBI Test; TBI test unavailable and household contact
- Perform TBI Test -> Positive; Negative; Indeterminate
- Positive -> Start TPT
- Negative -> No TPT
- Indeterminate -> No TPT
- TBI test unavailable and household contact -> Start TPT
Neither CXR nor a TB infection (TBI) test is mandatory to decide to start TPT. Other risk groups: silicosis, immunosuppressive drugs (long steroid therapy, cancer chemotherapy), anti-TNF treatment, transplantation (including candidates), health care workers and offenders.

heading_path: Chapter 11: Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment > 11.8 TPT Regimens and Dosing > Table 58: TPT Regimens and Dosing for PLHIV
text:
### Table 58: TPT regimens and dosing for people living with HIV: 3HP (preferred, ≥12 years and ≥25 kg), 1HP alternative, 6H for children <14 years or <30 kg and pregnant women, isoniazid mg/kg by age, vitamin B6

| Population group | Preferred regimen | Alternative regimen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Individuals ≥12 years and ≥25 kg | 3HP\*: weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months (rifapentine 300 mg/isoniazid 300 mg per tablet, 12 doses) – 3 tablets weekly plus 25 or 50 mg [as printed] plus vitamin B6 weekly | 1HP (when available): daily isoniazid plus rifapentine for 1 month. Dosage: 300 mg isoniazid and 600 mg rifapentine daily plus 25 mg vitamin B6 daily |
| Children <14 years or weight <30 kg | 6H: 6 months of daily isoniazid plus vitamin B6 25 mg daily. Isoniazid dosing: <10 years 10 mg/kg/day; >10 years 5 mg/kg/day | 3HP/1HP may be used for ≥2 years old when a child-friendly formula is available. |
| Pregnant women | 6H: 6 months of daily isoniazid plus vitamin B6 25 mg daily (dosing 5 mg/kg/day, maximum 300 mg/day). PNP prophylaxis for INH-containing regimen: vitamin B6 10-25 mg/day | — |

**Note:** 3HP is not recommended for PLHIV taking antiretrovirals with clinically significant or unknown drug interactions with rifapentine, or for people presumed infected with isoniazid- or rifampicin-resistant M. tuberculosis. In infants receiving NVP for prevention of mother-to-child transmission, 6H should be the preferred regimen; caregivers of exposed infants who complete PMTCT should be told that if the infant becomes HIV positive, TPT may need to change from 3HR to avoid drug interactions.

Population groupPreferred regimenAlternative regimen
Individuals ≥12 years and ≥25 kg3HP*: weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months (rifapentine 300 mg/isoniazid 300 mg per tablet, 12 doses) – 3 tablets weekly plus 25 or 50 mg [as printed] plus vitamin B6 weekly1HP (when available): daily isoniazid plus rifapentine for 1 month. Dosage: 300 mg isoniazid and 600 mg rifapentine daily plus 25 mg vitamin B6 daily
Children <14 years or weight <30 kg6H: 6 months of daily isoniazid plus vitamin B6 25 mg daily. Isoniazid dosing: <10 years 10 mg/kg/day; >10 years 5 mg/kg/day3HP/1HP may be used for ≥2 years old when a child-friendly formula is available.
Pregnant women6H: 6 months of daily isoniazid plus vitamin B6 25 mg daily (dosing 5 mg/kg/day, maximum 300 mg/day). PNP prophylaxis for INH-containing regimen: vitamin B6 10-25 mg/day—
3HP is not recommended for PLHIV taking antiretrovirals with clinically significant or unknown drug interactions with rifapentine, or for people presumed infected with isoniazid- or rifampicin-resistant M. tuberculosis. In infants receiving NVP for prevention of mother-to-child transmission, 6H should be the preferred regimen; caregivers of exposed infants who complete PMTCT should be told that if the infant becomes HIV positive, TPT may need to change from 3HR to avoid drug interactions.

text:
### Table 59: Documented adverse events with drug used for TPT (Adverse event, Responsible drug, Management) | Adverse event | Responsible drug | Management | | --- | --- | --- | | Flu-like signs and symptoms | Rifapentine, rifampicin | • Advise to stay hydrated by drinking plenty of water and juice.
• Prescribe Paracetamol which may be taken every 4 to 6 hours. Leave at least 4 hours between doses. (Dosage 500mg tab for adults, for children 3 months- 6 years 120mg/5ml suspension, children 6 years of age and adults 250mg/5ml suspension.)
• If severe and not tolerated to 3HP/3HR regimen, consider switching to an alternate regimen (6H) | | Nausea and
vomiting | Rifapentine, rifampicin,
isoniazid | • Prescribe 10 mg of metoclopramide bid (twice a day) or
tid.
• Advise patients to stay hydrated by drinking plenty of
water and juice.
• Avoid spicy and greasy foods.
• Prescribe oral rehydration solution if mild dehydration is
present. | | Hepatotoxicity | More with INH than
rifapentine and rifampicin) | • If people on TPT have signs and symptoms of
hepatotoxicity, perform LFT.
• If aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and/or alanine
aminotransferase (ALT) are >3 but <5 times upper limit of
normal (ULN) without signs and symptoms of hepatitis,
continue TPT and repeat AST and ALT weekly.
• If AST and/or ALT >3 times ULN with signs and symptoms
of hepatitis or if AST and/or ALT >5 times ULN with or
without signs and symptoms of hepatitis, stop TPT and do
not reintroduce. | | Peripheral
neuropathy | Isoniazid | • Use brief peripheral neuropathy scoring system
(BPNS) to screen and assess the severity of peripheral
neuropathy.
• If mild: give 100 to 150 mg of pyridoxine in adults and 50
mg in children.
• If not better or worsened with an increased pyridoxine
dose, stop the H-containing regimen and consider
switching to 4R. | | Skin
hypersensitivity
reaction | Rifampicin, Rifapentine,
Isoniazid | • If itchiness and localized mild rashes occur, give calamine
lotion or steroid cream to apply bid on the affected area;
chlorpheniramine 8 mg tid or bid orally may be given.
• If itchiness, generalized rashes, or swelling of oral or nasal
mucosa with or without fever, withhold TPT.
• For mild or moderate hypersensitivity reaction,
desensitization may be attempted with a low dose rechallenge once the rash resolves starting with isoniazid
alone at 1/6 normal dose on day 1, then full dose on day
2 and subsequently monitoring closely, especially on the
completion of antihistamines (at least weekly to 2-weekly
for the first month then monthly).
• If a rash does not recur, continue isoniazid monotherapy
ensuring that the client gets a total of 180 doses.
If rash recurs, do not rechallenge with isoniazid.
Alternative regimen 4R may be considered by re-introduction with a low dose (1/6 of the dose) on day 1 and then a full dose on day 2.
• If desensitization cannot be performed, an alternative regimen (e.g. 4R or 6H) may be considered
• Never reintroduce after severe hypersensitivity reaction or Stevens-Johnson syndrome. | | Orange-red discoloration of body fluid (tear, saliva, urine, milk, urine) | Rifampicin, rifapentine | • Reassure that it is just the staining from a drug in the regimen and is harmless. Advice to continue TPT. | | Any occurrence of TB signs and symptoms | | • Investigate for active TB disease or other diseases.
• If there is no active TB disease, continue TPT.
• If active TB disease, stop TPT and provide DS-TB or DR-TB treatment, as appropriate. |

Orange-red discoloration of body fluid (tear, saliva, urine, milk, urine)Rifampicin, rifapentine• Reassure that it is just the staining from a drug in the regimen and is harmless. Advice to continue TPT.

heading_path: 11.13 TPT completion and management of TBI treatment interruption > Table 62: Management of TPT interruption or missed dose
text:
### Table 62: Management of TPT interruption or missed dose (TPT regimen, Duration of treatment interruption, Next Steps) Table 62: Management of TPT interruption or missed dose | TPT regimen | Duration of treatment interruption | Next Steps | | --- | --- | --- | | 3HP | 1 weekly dose missed
More than 1 weekly doses missed | If the missed dose is remembered within the next 2 days, continue to take the remaining doses according to the original schedule. If the missed dose is remembered > 2 days later, take the missed dose immediately, and change the schedule for weekly intake to the day the missed dose was taken, until treatment completion. This will avoid 2 weekly doses being taken fewer than 4 days apart.
If treatment interruption occurred after at least 9 doses were taken within 12 weeks of starting, continue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 112 days. If ≥ 4 weekly doses are missed, consider restarting the full TPT course. If an individual has difficulty adhering to a weekly routine, consider dis continuing 3HP and offering an alternative regimen with daily dosing. | | 1HP | Less than 7 doses missed
More than 7 doses missed | Continue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 6 weeks (42 days from starting TPT)
If < 7 consecutive doses were missed, consider restarting the complete course of the 1HP regimen. If > 7 doses were missed intermittently, continue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 6 weeks (42 days from starting TPT) | | 3HR, 4R, 6H, 6Lfx | Less than 2 weeks
More than 2 weeks | Resume TPT and add the number of missed doses to the total treatment duration.
Do not change the scheduled date of the next follow-up visit, but postpone the last follow-up visit by the number of extra days to compensate for missed doses. For example, if a child on 3HR misses 3 days of treatment, continue TPT for a total of 3 months + 3 days from the date of start.
If treatment interruption occurs after more than 80% of doses in the regimen have been taken, continue and complete the remaining treatment as per the original plan. If less than 80% of doses in the regimen were taken, and the treatment course can still be completed within the expected treatment duration + 33% additional time, continue and complete the remaining treatment as per the original plan. For example, if an adult on 6H had taken only 120 doses by month 6, the remaining 62 doses can be taken in the next 2 months, without exceeding the 239-day limit. If < 80% of doses in the regimen were taken, and the treatment course cannot be completed within the expected time, consider restarting the full TPT course. A shorter regimen would be preferable. |

text:
### 16.1 Community Referrals and Linkages (Special Considerations for the diagnosis of TB in children:)

| Special Considerations for the diagnosis of TB in children: |
| --- |
| • Write down a facility-to-facility referral form for the child |
| • Call the facility where the child will be referred to and schedule an appointment |
| • Appoint the child for follow-up in the referring facility appointment register |
| • After the day of the agreed date to visit the facility, call the facility to follow up if client has honoured the appointment |
| • Follow up with the caregiver if the child did not reach the health facility and reappoint in the facility appointment register |
